The retail orders database has three tables. Each order is one customer
buying one product. `customer_id` and `product_id` in `orders` point back to
the `customers` and `products` tables.

Answer each question **by hand**, using only the tables below. Write your
answer as a small table or a number. Later you will write a SQL query for
each question and check your answers on the
[database](https://calvinw.github.io/FIT-courses/CS211/lectures/sql/create-retail-orders-brief-db.sql).

## The tables

**customers**

| customer_id | first_name | last_name |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | John | Doe |
| 2 | Jane | Smith |
| 3 | Robert | Johnson |
| 4 | Sarah | Williams |

**products**

| product_id | name | price |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Silk Blouse | 89.99 |
| 2 | Denim Jeans | 79.99 |
| 3 | Cashmere Sweater | 149.99 |
| 4 | Cotton T-Shirt | 29.99 |
| 5 | Wool Coat | 199.99 |

**orders**

| order_id | customer_id | product_id | order_date |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 3 | 2025-03-10 |
| 2 | 2 | 1 | 2025-03-12 |
| 3 | 3 | 4 | 2025-03-15 |
| 4 | 2 | 4 | 2025-03-18 |
| 5 | 1 | 2 | 2025-03-20 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 2025-03-25 |
